title: When You Accidentally Open the Front Camera
description:
Duration: 12–16 seconds
Format: 9:16 YouTube Shorts
Genre: Relatable 3D Animated Comedy
Style: Awkward, deadpan, mostly silent visual humor

Story Description

Doug is relaxing on his couch in his living room, casually scrolling through his phone. He looks comfortable, slightly bored, and completely unaware of what's about to happen.

Scene 1 — Casual Scrolling (0–3s)

Doug is sitting comfortably on the couch, holding his smartphone.

He casually taps around his phone with his usual half-lidded, relaxed expression.

Suddenly, he accidentally opens the camera app in selfie mode.

The screen instantly displays his face from an extremely unflattering low angle.

Scene 2 — The Horrifying Discovery (3–6s)

Show a close-up of the phone screen.

Doug's face appears ridiculously distorted by the camera perspective: an oversized forehead, exaggerated nostrils, awkward double chin, and terrible lighting.

The image should clearly be Doug himself, not a different character.

Cut back to Doug staring at his phone.

His eyes slowly widen in disbelief.

He blinks once.

Then looks at the screen again.

Scene 3 — Checking Reality (6–10s)

Doug slowly raises the phone to a more flattering angle.

His face on the screen looks normal again.

He lowers the phone.

The horrifying low-angle face returns.

He raises it again.

Normal.

Lowers it again.

Horrifying.

Doug pauses, staring at the screen with silent disappointment.

Scene 4 — Final Punchline (10–15s)

Doug slowly turns off his phone.

He places it face down on the couch beside him.

He sits perfectly still for a moment, processing what he just witnessed.

Then he quietly picks up a nearby blanket and pulls it over his head.

Hold for a brief awkward silence.

Cut to black.

Character and Animation Requirements

Preserve Doug's exact existing yellow 3D character design, orange hat, eyes, mouth, and body proportions.

The front-camera image must show the same Doug model, distorted only through camera perspective.

Avoid generating a different face or character on the phone screen.

Use natural eye tracking, subtle blinking, and understated reactions.

Doug should remain mostly deadpan rather than screaming or overreacting.

Keep body movements smooth and physically believable.

Ensure the phone remains properly attached to his hand without clipping or floating.

Camera Direction

Use clear, simple shots:

Medium shot of Doug scrolling on the couch.

Close-up of the phone showing the unflattering selfie.

Close-up of Doug's reaction.

Alternating phone angles showing the visual difference.

Wide shot of Doug hiding under the blanket.

Keep the editing tight and avoid excessive cuts.

Audio Direction

No dialogue from Doug.

Subtle phone tapping sounds.

A small camera activation sound.

Brief awkward silence during Doug's reaction.

Soft blanket movement at the ending.

No narration or unnecessary sound effects.

Comedy Direction

The humor should come from the contrast between how Doug normally looks and how terrible the accidental front-camera angle makes him appear.

The camera-angle comparison must be visually obvious.

Avoid excessive facial expressions or forced jokes.

The final blanket reaction should feel like Doug silently deciding he's had enough of seeing himself for the day.

Final Validation

Before finalizing, verify that:

Doug's original character design remains consistent.

The phone clearly switches to the front camera.

The selfie looks like Doug, not another character.

The flattering and unflattering angles are visibly different.

The phone and hands maintain proper physical contact.

The final blanket action is clear and natural.

The punchline works without dialogue.

The final video is approximately 12–16 seconds.

Core joke: Doug accidentally sees himself through the front camera at the worst possible angle, questions his entire appearance, and silently hides from the world.

revisions.text:
Revise the existing V1 animation of **"When You Accidentally Open the Front Camera"** for Deadpan Doug. Make targeted improvements only. Preserve the original character models, 3D art style, living room environment, and blanket ending.

**1. FIX LEGS AND FEET CLIPPING THROUGH THE COUCH — CRITICAL**

Doug's legs and feet are visibly intersecting and passing through the couch geometry.

- Correct Doug's sitting pose, hip height, knee positions, and foot placement.
- His body should rest naturally on the couch cushion, with his legs positioned correctly in front of the seat.
- Ensure his feet do not penetrate the couch, cushions, or floor.
- Check the entire animation, not just the opening frame.
- Maintain proper contact between Doug's body and the couch while he moves, adjusts his phone, and reacts.
- Fix the actual character pose, rig, or geometry intersections. Do not hide clipping using camera angles.
- Preserve Doug's existing body proportions and the couch dimensions.

**2. FIX TITLE FONT AND TEXT READABILITY — HIGH PRIORITY**

The current title text is difficult to read and visually inconsistent with previous Deadpan Doug videos.

- Inspect the original text-rendering settings from previously approved episodes, especially the Barista and Bathroom videos.
- Reuse the exact established font family, weight, outline, size, and text placement wherever available.
- Do not guess the previous font or introduce a completely different typography style.
- If the original font is unavailable, use a clean, bold, highly readable sans-serif font such as Montserrat ExtraBold.
- Use high-contrast white lettering with a subtle black outline or shadow.
- Ensure text remains readable on mobile devices.
- Keep all text within YouTube Shorts' safe viewing area.
- Avoid thin lettering, excessive text animation, or decorative fonts.

**3. MAKE THE ACCIDENTAL FRONT CAMERA ACTIVATION CLEARER**

The current opening does not clearly establish that Doug accidentally activates the front-facing camera.

- Begin with Doug casually scrolling on his phone while sitting on the couch.
- Show his finger accidentally tapping the camera icon or switching to selfie mode.
- The phone screen should visibly change from normal content to the front-camera preview.
- Doug should initially be unaware of the accidental activation.
- After noticing his reflection, he should pause and slowly react.
- Keep the action natural and concise without adding unnecessary shots.

**4. IMPROVE THE GOOD-ANGLE VS. BAD-ANGLE COMPARISON**

The joke depends on Doug accidentally seeing himself from an extremely unflattering angle.

- Clearly establish the first unflattering low-angle selfie.
- Keep the phone screen showing Doug's exact existing character, not a redesigned or different character.
- Doug raises the phone to eye level, revealing a normal-looking version of himself.
- He lowers the phone again, returning to the exaggerated, unflattering angle.
- Repeat the comparison briefly if it improves comedic timing.
- Make the visual differences obvious through camera perspective, not inconsistent character models.
- Maintain realistic phone orientation and synchronized movement between Doug's hand and the selfie preview.
- Avoid changing Doug's actual facial geometry or permanent appearance.

**5. IMPROVE FACIAL EXPRESSIONS AND EYE TRACKING**

- Preserve Doug's signature half-lidded, deadpan expression.
- Add subtle eye movements as he examines his phone.
- His reaction should gradually progress from casual boredom to confusion, disbelief, and silent disappointment.
- Keep his mouth consistently visible.
- Avoid exaggerated expressions, robotic blinking, or unnatural eye movements.
- Ensure facial proportions remain consistent throughout every shot.

**6. IMPROVE PACING AND COMEDIC TIMING**

- Reduce repetitive selfie close-ups that do not contribute to the joke.
- Make the progression clear: casual scrolling → accidental selfie → horrifying low-angle view → angle comparison → silent
V2 Final Revision: seated pose on the cushion, obvious low-vs-eye-level selfie comparison, clear accidental tap, Barista/Bathroom title typography, keep face acting and blanket ending.

V3 Comedy Revision: FAHHH (owner-supplied sound) on every bad selfie reveal, none on the normal angle; stronger shock with head recoil; four angles low / eye level / too close / worst; freeze, 0.5 s silence, back to deadpan, blanket ending kept.

versions.notes: v1 (ep14), no dialogue, 15.8 s. Choices made unattended: reused the living-room set in evening lamp light with the TV off. The phone screen is a real render from the phone's front camera on the same Doug model, so only the angle and the cheap-camera grade (from the phone's own under-light) change. Doug has no nose, so there are no nostrils; the low angle gives the looming chin/body, a tiny face and a hat seen from below. The up/down comparison is shown from Doug's point of view so the screen stays readable. The blanket is draped over the couch back and pulled over his head (cloth sim). Sound: screen taps, a small camera-open blip, set-down, blanket rustle, room tone.

V2 final: Doug actually sits (thighs on the cushion, knees forward, shins down), one clear low → eye level → low selfie comparison, visible accidental tap with ripple and camera zoom-open, Barista/Bathroom title typography. Face acting and blanket ending kept.

V3 comedy: FAHHH on each bad selfie (accident low angle, too-close chin cam, worst belly cam), no sound on the normal eye-level view; head recoil and flinches; freeze with 0.5 s dead silence before the unchanged blanket ending.
